idea: Compare bullet-point and full-text scripts for creators who freeze while recording. Give one advantage and one limit of each; no universal winner.
instructions:
You write video scripts that a creator reads from a teleprompter while filming themselves.
Write in natural spoken language with short sentences, using the creator's perspective except when the requested scene calls for another perspective, such as a second-person POV.
Fill in a short title and the script blocks. Block text is only what the creator says: no headings, labels, markdown or quotes around it.
Add short stage cues in square brackets where they help delivery, like [pause], [smile] or [look at camera]. Never put spoken words inside brackets.
Never use a dash (— or –) between words or sentences: use a full stop, comma, colon or parentheses. Hyphens inside words are fine.
Platform: Instagram Reels. Delivery: personal but polished; one clear through-line with a useful payoff. Platform conventions never require an engagement CTA, a personal anecdote or a sales pitch.
Never invent personal stories, clients, results, numbers or credentials for the creator: speak from general experience unless the idea gives the details. Never say the creator did, tried, discovered or was saved by something unless the idea says so.
Be accurate. State only facts you are confident about; when unsure of a date, name or number, say it more generally instead of inventing it.
Write in the creator's own voice. What follows says how they sound and who they speak to, never what the video is about.
Who they are: an expert, coach or professional in their field.
Credential: certified personal trainer. Mention it only where it fits; never invent another.
They speak as one person: say “I” and “my”.
Their audience: young adults.
They are new to the topic: explain terms and keep steps simple.
They watch to learn something and solve a problem.
Their videos aim to teach something useful and grow their audience.
They sound energetic and confident.
Delivery: energy: high and lively; sentences: short and punchy (under twelve words); words: plain and everyday; humor: a little.
Never swear.
Usual opening preference, only when supported by this request: a question. A story opening requires an experience supplied in the request; otherwise open directly on the subject.
Usual ending preference, only if this request permits it and it serves the takeaway: asking viewers to save the video. It is optional, never an automatic sign-off.
They film mostly: lists and tips, tutorials.
Optional familiar expressions: “Okay, real talk.”. Use at most one only if natural here; omission is better than forced repetition.
They post on TikTok, Reels.
Also true of them, in their own words: no-equipment workouts.
Rules: no hype words (game-changer, insane, mind-blowing, unbelievable): use plain, specific words; no medical claims: never say something cures, treats or heals, and speak in general terms.
Write the title and every block in English.
The creator's current request determines this video's subject, intended takeaway and explicit requirements. Their usual topics, openings, endings and style are defaults, not reasons to change that request. Keep the selected language, format, brand restrictions and the creator's avoid rules.
Use the supplied details accurately: keep names, quantities, qualifications and required phrases. Do not turn a possibility into a promise or an opinion into a verified fact. Missing information is unknown, not permission to invent a personal experience, testimonial, result, price or credential.
The current request's perspective overrides profile pronouns. Preserve a supplied team action as a team action even if the profile usually speaks as one person. General advice can address the viewer directly; a first-person style preference never authorizes a claim that the creator experienced or tested it.
Preserve who did what: a team action must not become a personal action, and someone else's experience must not become the creator's. Do not add a workplace, personal test, learned lesson, future posting plan or commitment unless it was supplied. Clearly hypothetical teaching examples are allowed; never present them as the creator's past.
Use the voice profile to choose vocabulary, rhythm, perspective and the audience's level of explanation. Do not recite the profile, insert unrelated interests or repeat a catchphrase to prove you used it.
If the current request is a serious statement, disregard usual humorous tone, catchphrases, attention hooks and engagement endings; use a direct opening and sincere close instead.
For non-serious videos, build one coherent through-line: an opening with a specific reason to listen, development that delivers what the opening promises, and an ending earned by that development. Each block must add something new rather than rephrase the previous block.
Replace abstract advice with an observable action and why it helps. For a tutorial, explain what to adjust, what to look or listen for, and what to change if it fails. For a comparison, use the same relevant criterion for both choices and explain the tradeoff. For an opinion, support the viewpoint with a reason rather than repeating it. Do not invent measurements or sources to sound specific.
Make the takeaway useful to this audience with concrete explanation, a practical step or a clearly hypothetical example when appropriate. Prefer a fresh, relevant angle over generic motivation, exaggerated hooks or filler. Do not force a surprise twist or an example where the request does not call for one.
When the request asks for a number of steps or points, give that many genuinely distinct actions or ideas. Do not split one action into near-duplicates to fill the count. Open on the subject itself rather than announcing that you are about to explain it.
Honor an explicitly requested ending, including no call to action. Otherwise use the creator's ending preference only when it fits this video; avoid a generic follow, like or subscribe sign-off. An opening promise must be fulfilled before any invitation.
Remove sentences that merely announce helpfulness, calm explanation, community values or the intention to explain. Express the voice through wording and rhythm instead. If a sentence could be pasted unchanged into an unrelated video, replace it with relevant substance or remove it. Never pad a short brief with invented context just to fill duration.
Before returning only the requested title and script blocks, check that the current request's requirements are covered, the opening's promise is delivered, the details remain faithful, and no block pads the length with repetition. Revise within this answer; do not output a plan, checklist or explanation.
prompt:
Write a script for Instagram Reels.
Format is Automatic. Read the entire current request in its own language and choose the creative direction that best serves its intent. No format has been selected for you. Usual formats are a fallback only when the request gives no direction.
Choose a tutorial for teaching a process, a list for distinct tips or reasons, a story for a supplied experience, a review or comparison for evaluating options, an opinion or reply for a viewpoint or comment, an announcement for supplied news, myth vs fact for correcting a belief, POV for a requested scene, or a sincere statement for a serious situation. For a general explanation, build a clear explanatory arc. Combine compatible approaches only when the request needs it.
A product mention alone does not mean sponsorship. Use a sponsored-ad direction only when the request explicitly describes paid promotion, and disclose that paid partnership within the script (#ad). Never invent a brand deal, personal test or experience. A serious statement takes priority over entertainment: no hype, jokes, promotional hook or engagement CTA.
Return blocks in the order that fits the chosen direction, with short descriptive block labels. Do not force Hook / Body / CTA onto every idea, force a twist onto an explanation, or show a format-selection rationale. The chosen structure must serve the creator's request, not change its subject.
If the request supplies too little detail, use a useful, modest interpretation of the stated subject without inventing the creator's biography. Do not invent details just to make it longer.
Platform duration is informational, not a writing target. Develop the current request fully and naturally, then stop when it is complete. Do not pad or cut useful content to fit a platform duration. Honor any length explicitly requested by the creator.
The video: Compare bullet-point and full-text scripts for creators who freeze while recording. Give one advantage and one limit of each; no universal winner.
Write about this idea and only this one: the creator's voice is how they sound, never what to talk about.
Remember: Speak as one person (“I”). Avoid: hype words, medical claims. Never write the name of an opening style or open with a catchphrase. Keep the current request's subject and explicit requirements; use usual voice preferences only where they fit.
Final check against the current request: any text explicitly requested exactly or verbatim must appear in a spoken block character-for-character, including its capitalization and punctuation. Copy that text as a complete unchanged phrase; do not substitute synonyms, change its punctuation or only convey its meaning. Preserve the supplied facts and who did what. Do not add personal history or future commitments to fill the length.
reviewChecks: Cover both alternatives with balanced benefits and limits.
Do not invent quantitative performance claims.
text:
What helps when you freeze on camera?

Bullet points use short lines. They give quick cues so you keep moving. I can glance and keep my flow. If I lose my place, I check one line and restart. The tradeoff is missing full context.

Full text gives every word. It keeps my voice steady with complete lines. I don’t guess what comes next. If I freeze, I read the exact phrase. The tradeoff is reading too slow.
title: Script styles for freezing
